chunks.text: 2 Methods This section details our FloVMos implementation. We first outline the FloVMos framework in Sec. 2.1 and then describe our novel synthetic data-based training method and each framework component in Sections 2.2 - 2.5 . These sections are followed by our approach to handle video stream jumps (Sec. 2.6 ) and our salient-points-based method for assessing mosaicking accuracy without ground truth (Sec. 2.7 ). Finally, Sec. 2.8 details the data used in our experiments. 2.1 Brief Description of FloVMos operation FloVMos is illustrated in Fig. 2 . As shown in the figure and described in the caption, FloVMos first undergoes a training process where the parameters of the optical flow DNN are fine-tuned to a particular modality. This training uses pairs of images from the modality of interest, which are related to each other by known optical flow parameters. Our procedures to automatically extract this training data from existing mosaics or videos from that modality are described in detail in Sec. 2 . Once the DNN has been fine-tuned, FloVMos is ready to process newly acquired videos. First, the optical flow DNN estimates optical flow between each new frame and “a cropped region-of-interest” covering the most recently acquired frame already integrated into the mosaic. The registered images are then added to the existing mosaic by blending the new frame with the existing mosaic. This process is repeated on each frame until the end of the video. If any abrupt jump (e.g., motion blur, depth changes) is detected, based on an abrupt loss of optical flow smoothness as detailed in Sec. 2.6 , we either modify the mosaicking process to overcome the jump or, if that is not feasible, terminate the videomosaicing process, saving the existing mosaic, and begin a new mosaic starting from that image frame. Figure 2: Overview of FloVMos : a The first step in training involves the acquisition of training data.

We have developed two approaches for easy, rapid, and automated acquisition of the required training data. In the first, when sample mosaics are easily available, we simply simulate videos by following a randomized but known path through the mosaic and then adding noise and distortion, as illustrated in the figure. In the second, when we only have videos available, we randomly choose or simulate pairs of images from the video, again with known relationships between the elements of each pair, and add noise and distortion. In both cases, we can thus assemble a collection of labeled pairs of images to use as training data. b We fine-tune the optical flow neural network using the annotated training data. c After training, we apply the DNN to newly acquired (or “test”) videos. The video frames are registered using DNN-predicted optical flow and then assembled into a mosaic by our graph-cuts based stitching algorithm. appending each registered image to the growing mosaic. 2.2 Automated Generation of Training Data Accurate image registration underpins all video mosaicking techniques, serving as a critical foundation for downstream processing. Optical flow-based registration, which estimates dense, pixel-wise displacement fields, is particularly well-suited to capturing the complex non-rigid deformations frequently observed in medical imaging. However, state-of-the-art optical flow models trained on everyday scenes often produce large errors or fail entirely when applied to domain-specific medical data. To address this gap, we developed an automated training data generation framework that produces synthetic video sequences paired with ground-truth optical flow annotations. This framework simulates realistic camera motion and tissue deformation, enabling effective domain adaptation of optical flow estimators to a wide range of imaging modalities.

In some applications, large field-of-view images may already be available, either through an alternative version of the imaging device or generated using specialized offline programs specifically developed for the target application. For example, in one of our modalities of interest, reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) imaging of skin, it is possible to collect mosaic images using an articulated arm configuration of the microscope, which latches to the area of interest and moves the objective lens over the imaging area in a controlled fashion (e.g., via a raster or strip scan). In another modality, open-top light-sheet (OTLS) microscopy, data is acquired in large-scale mosaic volumes by mounting multiple optically cleared specimens on a flat transparent holder, with both the illumination and collection objectives positioned beneath the imaging plane. For these modalities, we simulate videos by simulating the path of a limited FOV device across a given larger mosaic, starting at a random location in the interior of the large FOV image and following a randomized path with controlled random parameters. Since the process is randomized, we can repeat it many times to acquire as large a set of simulated videos as desired. For modalities where only videos are available, in which each individual image (frame) has a limited field of view, we simulated the acquisition of image pairs with known optical flow relationships using individual video frames in two different ways. The first method involves randomly selecting a single frame from a video and tiling this frame into a 2 × 2 2\times 2 grid of frames by flipping the frame vertically and horizontally, resulting in smooth, synthetic “mini-mosaics” that are twice the size of the original frames along each dimension.The second method involves randomly selecting four frames that are temporally distant (at least 15% of the video’s total length apart) from each other within the video sequence.

We further (manually or automatically) ensure that there is less than 25% overlapping area between each of these selected frames to prevent duplicating nearby regions, in order to minimize potential confusion during optical flow training. These four frames are then again arranged into a 2 × 2 2\times 2 grid.While these simulated mini-mosaics may often appear unrealistic we found that they serve as a practical alternative for training data acquisition when large field-of-view images or mosaics are not available. These larger field-of-view images, whichever way they are acquired, can then be used to generate multiple synthetic videos with optical flow annotation. The synthetic data generation process starts by randomly selecting a location within the mosaic and extracting the initial frame matching the field of view of the target imaging modality. The rectangular area covered by this first frame serves as the initial synthetic camera view. Subsequent frames are generated by first randomly synthesizing an optical flow map that mimics both camera motion and the potential non-rigid deformations commonly observed during data acquisition. Using this optical flow map, we perform backward warping to produce the next frame. This process is repeated—generating a new optical flow map and corresponding frame—until the synthetic camera view reaches the edge of the mosaic. Note that for the first method, where simulated videos are extracted from large FOV mosaics, there will be many frames in the simulated video, while for the second method, where we start with a 2 × 2 2\times 2 synthetic image, there will be far fewer frames in each video. However, by repeatedly applying both processes to construct these 2 × 2 2\times 2 grids, we can still acquire as many image pairs for training as desired.

In more detail, each optical flow map used in either approach is randomly constructed by combining a global affine transformation (represented by a homography [ 11 ] ) with a denser non-rigid deformation field. (All parameters defined below are chosen using the values shown in Table 2.2 .) The affine component is parameterized by translation, rotation, and shearing. To ensure smooth and realistic camera motion, we adopt an autoregressive motion model, in which the translation and rotation parameters at each step are conditioned on both the values from the previous step and a newly sampled random speed for the current step. The parameters are chosen as follows: Translation speed parameters are sampled from a uniform distribution within predefined bounds, denoted as Min Trans. and Max Trans. . Rotation speed and shearing are applied with probabilities sampled from uniform distributions in the ranges [ 0 , Max Rot. ] [0,\text{Max Rot.}] and [ 0 , Max Shear ] [0,\text{Max Shear}] . In order to simulate non-rigid deformations, we then deform the rigid optical flow field on a frame by frame basis by adding a smooth noise field to it with a preset probability P non-rigid P_{\text{non-rigid}} . To ensure the smoothness of the noise field, we first generate it as a coarse field of size 4 × 4 4\times 4 where the coefficients are drawn from a uniform distribution within the range [ − Non-Rigid Level , Non-Rigid Level ] [-\textit{Non-Rigid Level},\allowbreak\textit{Non-Rigid Level}] (see Table 2.2 for parameter values). We then upsample this coarse field to the size of the camera FOV via bilinear interpolation, ensuring the noise field is smooth. As the variance of the noise increases, the non-rigid deformations introduced in the generated data also increase. This combination of projective transformation and non-rigid deformation allows us to generate the optical flow field between each pair of consecutive synthetic video frames. By varying the parameters governing the projective transformations and non-rigid deformations during the data generation process, we can tailor the camera motion, speed, and degree of non-rigid distortion to match the characteristics of different imaging modalities. For example, using the degree of non-rigid deformation as an example, we can compare dermoscopy with RCM. In dermoscopy, the imaging process typically involves a stable contact between the device and the skin surface, resulting in relatively minor non-rigid motion artifacts. Therefore, we set the Non-Rigid Level to three for this modality. In contrast, reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) often involves handheld operation and imaging at higher magnification, which can lead to significant non-rigid motion due to subtle tissue deformation or hand-induced jitter. To reflect this greater variability, we set the Non-Rigid Level to 10 for RCM.

We similarly set other parameters, including translation, rotation, and shearing, based on prior knowledge or empirical observations specific to each modality. Our base DNN was FlowNet2 [ 13 ] , but as we describe in Sec. 3.5 , we also tested with three additional optical flow DNNs ( RAFT [ 24 ] , GMFlow [ 26 ] , and FlowFormer [ 12 ] ) to assess how sensitive FloVMos is to the specific choice of DNN. The base FlowNet2 model weights were obtained from its official PyTorch repository ( https://github.com/NVIDIA/flownet2-pytorch ). All four of these models are publicly available with pre-trained coefficients. We used the training data to adapt these pre-trained coefficients for each of the seven imaging modalities we tested, in each case starting from the published model coefficients.

We trained each model on a computer equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti X GPU with 11GB VRAM, AMD Ryzen 3900X, and 32 GB of memory. We used a batch size of 8 for FlowNet2 and GMFlow and 6 for RAFT and FlowFormer . These batch sizes were the maximum that fit within the 11 GB VRAM limit for each model. We employed the Adam optimizer [ 14 ] with an initial learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , for 100 epochs. To speed up the training process, we resized the images to 256 pixels × \times 256 pixels for all models. The original resolutions for different modalities are as follows: dermoscopy, RCM, SSM, and OTLS each have a resolution of 1000 × \times 1000 pixels; endoscopy videos are typically acquired at a resolution of 1280 × 1024 1280\times 1024 pixels; the resolutions for fetoscopy and laparoscopy vary depending on the specific implementation: fetoscopy videos range from 380 × 380 380\times 380 to 720 × 720 720\times 720 pixels, while laparoscopy videos range from 320 × 240 320\times 240 to 720 × 288 720\times 288 pixels. The result of this fine-tuning is a modality-adapted DNN optical flow estimator that we then applied to incoming image pairs to estimate the optical flow transformation for image-to-mosaic registration, as described next. 2.4 Image to Mosaic Registration Once we have estimated optical flow parameters between all pairs of consecutive images in a video, we could have taken a naive approach and simply register all images to the first frame. However, this method requires us to update the optical flow field recursively, and as we progress through the video, small errors at each step of the optical flow estimation process can accumulate and even potentially lead to a complete stitching failure [ 15 ] . To mitigate such an accumulation of registration errors, we instead registered each frame directly into the growing mosaic.

In other words, during the mosaic-building process, instead of using consecutive video frames to estimate the registration parameters, we apply the DNN to estimate optical flow between the incoming video frame and a cropped, rotated rectangular region from the latest version of the mosaic that corresponds to the most recently stitched frame. Specifically, we track the center and corners of the last stitched frame within the mosaic to estimate its translation and rotation relative to the mosaic coordinate system. Using these transformations, we crop the corresponding ROI from the mosaic and compute the optical flow between the new frame and this reference region. Once we have the requisite optical flow parameters, we apply inverse translation and rotation to map the registered frame back to the mosaic coordinate system. This means that the pipeline depicted in the “inference” panel in Fig. 2 is traversed in its entirety for every frame of the video, but because of our fast, GPU-assisted implementation, we are able to maintain mosaicking speed, as reported in Fig. 4 (c). 2.5 Image Warping and Graph-cut Based Stitching The pixel displacements generated by the optical flow model result in non-integer values for the pixel locations before warping. To resolve this issue, we need to interpolate to an integer-based grid using a scheme designed for non-rigid deformations. Thus, we adopted a bilinear interpolation scheme from the deformable convolution networks literature [ 3 ] . This approach allows us to handle the complexities of non-rigid deformations in the dense flow field, while maintaining the real-time performance essential for video mosaicking. Bilinear interpolation enables smooth sampling and interpolation of intensities from the new frame, ensuring accurate reconstruction of warped frame pixels onto the integer grid.

Specifically, the value x ⁡ ( p ) x(p) at the desired integer position p p can be calculated as the convolution with an interpolating kernel: x ⁡ ( p ) = ∑ q G ⁡ ( q , p ) ⋅ x ⁡ ( q ) x(p)=\sum_{q}G(q,p)\cdot x(q) (2) where p p and q q are two-dimensional locations in the plane and x ⁡ ( q ) x(q) represents the warped frame with fractional positions q q . The bilinear interpolation kernel G ⁡ ( q , p ) G(q,p) is defined as G ⁡ ( q , p ) = g ⁡ ( q x , p x ) ⋅ g ⁡ ( q y , p y ) G(q,p)=g(q_{x},p_{x})\cdot g(q_{y},p_{y}) , where g ⁡ ( a , b ) = max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − | a − b | ) g(a,b)=\max(0,1-|a-b|) . This formulation allows for real-time implementation of image interpolation, with a processing speed of approximately 35 frames per second (in a Python implementation running on the CPU of a regular workstation) on videos with a resolution of 1000 × \times 1000 pixels. Once the frame is registered to the mosaic ROI, we apply a graph-cut-based stitching algorithm we have previously developed in [ 15 ] , to merge the new frame with the mosaic. Briefly, this technique minimizes visual artifacts by stitching the mosaic and the new frame along an optimal seam, which is designed to pass through less detailed (low-pass signal) regions of the overlap between the mosaic and the new frame. The method retains the pixel values of the registered frame and thus avoids any blurring that might occur if we were instead to blend multiple pixel values. However, because the technique identifies a stitching seam between the mosaic and frames, the same pixel in the mosaic could be overwritten multiple times if it falls within the overlap region across more than two frames. In such cases, the final value of the pixel is determined during the graph-cut-based stitching process by whether it is on the mosaic or the latest relevant frame side of the seam. 2.6 Handling abrupt changes in the videos Abrupt motion of the imaging device can result in blurring and/or discontinuities in the video data.

Moreover, for 3D imaging modalities such as RCM imaging, abrupt changes in imaging depth can also lead to discontinuities between consecutive frames. These phenomena can lead to severe errors in stitching and ultimately compromise the entire mosaicking process. Our approach is to first detect these abrupt changes and then either use adjacent frames to maintain continuity if possible, or start a new mosaic if that is not possible. To accomplish this, we developed an efficient method to detect outlier frames using optical flow. We start by observing that, in the absence of abrupt changes, the warping field between consecutive images is non-rigid but smooth. However, when artifacts are present in image data, the optical flow estimator can mistakenly align non-corresponding, yet visually similar, features as it aims to minimize differences between two input images. To detect these irregularities, we employ a simple method that measures the smoothness of the optical flow by averaging a discrete estimate of the spatial second-order derivatives of the flow map. This smoothness metric helps us detect when the neural network’s outputs contain artifactual areas. Through empirical analysis—specifically by introducing artifacts until the optical flow network failed to produce a smooth flow—we determined a threshold value of 0.1 for flagging anomalous frames. Once a frame with artifactual areas is flagged, our pipeline first attempts to ensure the continuity of stitching by utilizing the optical flows from subsequent frames following the one that led to distorted flow. If the optical flow generated by a subsequent frame is artifact-free, as determined by this threshold, then the process continues from that frame, discarding the artifact-corrupted frame.

Specifically, to maintain continuity in video stitching, when abnormal optical flow is detected, we buffer a number of subsequent frames proportional to the video acquisition frame rate (e.g., buffering 1 second’s worth of frames). For each buffered frame, we compute its optical flow relative to the mosaic reference area and evaluate the smoothness of the flow field by calculating its mean second-order derivatives. The frame associated with the smoothest flow (i.e., lowest mean second-order derivatives) is then selected as the next valid frame for stitching, as it is likely to be the first normal frame following the artifact-corrupted frames. However, to ensure the reference frame and the frame selected from the buffer contain enough overlap (since they are not consecutive images in the video), the average pixel value difference between the mosaic region of interest and the warped frame is computed. If this difference exceeds an empirical threshold of 30 (for monochrome images) or 40 (for RGB images), instead of trying to combine that frame with the existing mosaic, we initiate a new mosaic starting from the last buffered frame. 2.7 Identifying Salient Points for Computing Registration Errors In the absence of the ground truth optical flows, it is not possible to quantitatively measure the accuracy of the registration. To address this problem, we developed a novel procedure to estimate registration accuracy. Our primary assumption is that the distance between structures in the frames should not change drastically in the mosaic after registration and warping. In this respect, we developed a method that compares the distance between matching salient points in the input videos and the reconstructed mosaics. Specifically, we extracted salient features from each video frame as well as the mosaic using the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [ 18 ] .

To establish correspondences, we applied a brute-force matcher to identify candidate matches between the SIFT keypoints of each frame and those of the mosaic. Given the characteristics of these images, including repeated or structurally similar patterns, erroneous matches are likely to occur. To ensure robustness, we employed the Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) algorithm [ 5 ] with 10,000 iterations to estimate a homography and identify inlier correspondences. Frames with fewer than 5% inliers, relative to the total number of detected features, were excluded from further analysis. Additionally, we constrained the estimated scaling factors of the homography—defined as the eigenvalues of the 2 × 2 2\times 2 top-left submatrix of the homography matrix—to lie within the range [ 0.8 , 1.25 ] [0.8,1.25] . Matches that produced scaling factors outside this range were considered outliers and subsequently discarded. After this verification of geometric consistency, we computed a pairwise distance matrix between the matched keypoints in the frame and the mosaic. The frame-wise displacement of salient features was then obtained by subtracting the distance matrix of the frame from that of the mosaic. This procedure was then repeated for every frame in the sequence to compute an averaged error metric. 2.8 Dataset Details We tested FloVMos using data from seven different imaging modalities. All RCM and dermoscopy images were collected at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). The OTLS microscopy mosaics and SSM videos were graciously provided by Northeastern University’s Spring Lab ( https://sites.google.com/view/springlabnu ) and the University of Washington’s Molecular Biophotonics Laboratory ( https://washington-seattle.digication.com/jonliu/Home ), respectively.

The endoscopy, laparoscopy, and fetoscopy videos were obtained from publicly available datasets (the Endoscopic Vision Challenge ( https://opencas.dkfz.de/endovis/challenges/2024/ ), Hamlyn Center Laparoscopic/Endoscopic Video ( https://hamlyn.doc.ic.ac.uk/vision/ ), and FetReg datasets ( https://www.ucl.ac.uk/interventional-surgical-sciences/weiss-open-research/weiss-open-data-server/fetreg-largescale-multi-centre-fetoscopy-placenta-dataset ), respectively). For the RCM and OTLS imaging modalities, we had large field-of-view mosaic images available that were generated using a non-handheld version of the image acquisition devices. These devices are capable of moving the sample with respect to the imaging device in a controlled fashion (e.g., raster scan, or strip scan [ 1 ] ), using additional hardware (e.g., a motorized stage), and generating mosaics by tiling the collected images. We used these mosaics to generate simulated mosaics as described above and used them either to obtain training data or for testing of our algorithm. Additionally, we had RCM videos that were recorded using a handheld device. These videos are used for testing the framework. For all the other experiments, we only had access to videos. 3 Results We present results that illustrate FloVMos ’ ability to easily and accurately mosaic data from diverse imaging modalities. We then report on three additional technical aspects of FloVMos ’ performance: its ability to handle non-rigid deformations, its mosaicking speed as a function of video sequence length, and its flexibility with regard to the specific optical flow DNN employed. 3.1 Applying FloVMos to videos from multiple imaging modalities We show results from the application of FloVMos on eight examples from seven different imaging modalities: fetoscopy, dermoscopy, reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM), endoscopy, sparse-spectral microendoscopy (SSM), laparoscopy, and open-top light sheet microscopy (OTLS). For RCM, videos are obtained using a handheld microscope, while mosaics are acquired directly with a different version of the microscope. For OTLS, the mosaics are captured by a bench-top scope. For other modalities, only videos without mosaics are available. Full details on the eight datasets are described in Sec. 2.8 and Table 2.8 . We illustrate the operation of FloVMos on all these datasets in Fig. 3 panels a through h . We also report quantitative results on all eight datasets in the bottom panel of Fig. 3 . Figure 3: Results of applying FloVMos to different imaging modalities: Top: FloVMos qualitative results are presented for eight cases from seven different imaging modalities: (a) Fetoscopy; (b) Dermoscopy; (c) real RCM; (d) SSM; (e) simulated RCM; (f) Endoscopy; (g) Laparoscopy) and (h) videos simulated from an OTLS mosaic. The red circle / box in each image shows the location of the first frame in the video.

(We use a red circle for the fetoscopy video to match the actual FOV of the device; when we use FloVMos to create a mosaic, the frames are stitched onto a black background.) Bottom: Histograms of distances (in pixels) between image feature point pairs in the source mosaics or video frames and their matches in the resulting FloVMos mosaic. To calculate quantitative results, we needed some form of “ground truth” accuracy. For the RCM and OTLS modalities, where we synthesized videos from available mosaics, we simply calculated pixel distances between matched salient point locations in the original mosaic and the reconstructed FloVMos mosaic. For the other modalities, where we did not have ground truth mosaics, we automatically identified matching salient points in the original video and the reconstructed mosaic and again calculated pixel distances for each case. (Details in Sec. 2.7 ). Histograms of the resulting pixel distances in the figure are shown for all seven modalities at the bottom of Fig. 3 . In the case of RCM we have both real videos and videos simulated from existing mosaics, so we show results for both cases in the figure. This capability will enable researchers or clinicians to make rapid decisions about where to acquire further images on the tissue being examined, streamlining the imaging process. By leveraging an optical flow-based deep neural network based dense image registration model, FloVMos effectively addresses the critical challenges for wide and easy applicability of videomosaicking for small FOV medical and biological imaging devices, achieving broad applicability across multiple imaging modalities while requiring minimal human effort to retrain for a given modality, robust registration under varying motion and tissue deformation scenarios, and effectively real-time processing. We emphasize that, aside from tuning a few training parameters, applying FloVMos is a completely automated process, from generating the training data from either existing mosaics or existing videos all the way through the creation of the reconstructed mosaics. Our results show that FloVMos can be readily applied to a variety of modalities: as reported here, we tested it on RCM, dermoscopy, endoscopy, fetoscope, OTLS, SSM, and laparoscopy. We believe that this is a broad enough range of modalities to suggest that FloVMos will work with other existing, or even not-as-yet-invented, modalities as well. We report that FloVMos not only achieved lower MSE values compared to comparison methods but also demonstrated improved robustness against increasing levels of non-rigid deformation. We speculate this is true at least in part because of the flexible non-linear processing in the DNN optical flow estimator. While two of the comparison algorithms, along with FloVMos , showed little variation in processing time with respect to video length (Note that AVM often collapsed midway through stitching when processing 50-framelength videos. As a result, in practice, it ended up stitching shorter segments, which likely contributed to the observed increase in average speed in Fig.

4 ), in contrast to the Parallax algorithm that went from 0.2 to 0.05 FPS as the video lengths increased, FloVMos was not only insensitive to video length but also much faster than the comparison algorithms, which we attribute both to our approach of only operating on the most recently stitched part of the growing mosaic and the highly parallelizable nature of the DNN optical flow model, which can be run on a GPU with very high efficiency. Finally, we saw that FloVMos is relatively robust to the choice of optical flow estimator and confirmed the efficacy of our fine-tuning retraining for both accuracy metrics and all optical flow estimators. Optical flow-based dense image registration [ 7 ] relies on pixel displacement predictions represented as vector fields. Given an optical flow field, in principle, we merely need to “invert” the vector field to map one image onto its predecessor. Using this approach for the kinds of images of interest here imposes stringent accuracy requirements on the model. Consequently, most publicly available optical flow models, which are typically designed for and trained on everyday images, fail to meet these precision demands. FloVMos uses a trainable registration model that can be adapted to the specific motion characteristics of each imaging modality. Drawing inspiration from synthetic datasets (e.g., Kitti [ 19 ] , Flying Chair [ 4 ] ), which leverage computer graphics techniques to generate optical flow fields between paired images, we developed an automated synthetic training data generation method that mimics the motion of an image acquisition device. This emulation of controlled camera motion makes it possible to extract video frames and optical flow pairs to then use in training to fine-tune an optical flow estimator, eliminating the need for labor-intensive pixel-level optical flow field annotations.

FloVMos , by employing deep learning, inherently benefits from larger and more diverse training datasets, much like other DNN approaches. However, acquiring extensive medical imaging datasets poses significant challenges due to patient privacy considerations, the high cost of specialized equipment, and the labor-intensive nature of data acquisition. Our automated training data generation strategy addresses this problem, but the dataset sizes attainable by FloVMos remain substantially smaller compared to typical deep-learning benchmarks, particularly when only raw videos are available. When real mosaics from the same modality are available, larger synthetic datasets can be efficiently generated because these mosaics typically cover substantially larger tissue areas than single videos, thus providing richer data for training.

Users should be aware, however, that, models fine-tuned on limited datasets may exhibit biases, necessitating the incorporation of inductive biases—domain-specific prior knowledge—into both data generation and model training. Extending FloVMos to new imaging modalities depends critically on generating synthetic training data that closely resembles real data in terms of both image characteristics and optical flow patterns associated with camera motion. Our synthetic training methodology reliably captures general image features; however, additional modality-specific post-processing is typically required. For instance, circular masking replicates dark peripheral regions characteristic of fetoscopy, while carefully emulating illumination conditions can significantly improve realism for modalities with non-uniform lighting. A particularly challenging aspect of synthetic data generation involves accurately simulating camera motion and non-rigid deformation, as this strongly influences registration performance. The level of non-rigid deformation in simulations must reflect realistic scenarios specific to the target modality. For example, modalities involving substantial parallax (e.g., laparoscopy, endoscopy) or direct tissue contact (e.g., reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM)) tend to experience pronounced non-rigid deformations, whereas stable setups (e.g., open-top light-sheet microscopy (OTLS)) typically exhibit smaller deformations. Selecting suitable distortion parameters is thus crucial and ideally should be informed by prior domain knowledge. However, when such prior knowledge is limited or unavailable, a practical strategy involves generating an initial small dataset with varying deformation levels and qualitatively evaluating these against actual modality-specific data. This preliminary evaluation typically requires examining only a small set of synthetic examples to determine the extent of distortion introduced by different parameter settings.

In contrast, when only mosaic images are available, increasing the size and diversity of the synthetic dataset helps mitigate the uncertainty arising from the absence of direct temporal reference. Although iterative validation under these circumstances can be challenging, our empirical results confirm that adopting this strategy successfully yields effective synthetic training datasets, substantially improving the accuracy and robustness of FloVMos across diverse imaging scenarios. Finally, another practical consideration for achieving effective real-time deployment of FloVMos is video frame rate management. Empirically, we observed robust optical flow estimation with at least 50% overlap between consecutive frames. If high-frame-rate input videos have greater overlap, selective downsampling can substantially accelerate processing without compromising accuracy. While reliance on simulated data allows us to automatically tune our optical flow algorithm, it is also a major limitation of the current implementation of FloVMos . In particular, in the current study, we concentrated on close-proximity modalities. Clearly, there is a need for further testing in more general imaging modalities where the imaging device is farther from the tissue. Such modalities may introduce additional distortions that are not accounted for by our current data simulation model. To ensure robust clinical applicability, future studies should ideally test FloVMos on real-world clinical data and fine-tune the model as necessary, including the distortion parameters used to generate training data, to adapt to unique characteristics of a particular clinical or laboratory setting. Another limitation of the current FloVMos pipeline is its necessity for a GPU for real-time processing. While FloVMos runs well on affordable commercial GPUs, most clinical imaging systems do not meet this requirement.

One potential solution is to replace the existing optical flow model with one that operates efficiently on CPUs or to use model compression techniques like pruning, quantization, or knowledge distillation [ 10 , 9 ] . However, our DNN model’s flexibility and GPU implementation offer robust and fast performance, leaving the trade-offs of using a CPU or non-DNN model uncertain. One promising application of FloVMos is in intraoperative imaging systems, where real-time feedback can enhance surgical guidance. While our early studies indicate feasibility [ 27 , 6 ] , further research is needed to evaluate FloVMos ’s full potential and limitations in real-time settings. Future work should assess both the technical robustness of FloVMos under clinical conditions and its influence on surgical outcomes and workflow efficiency. We plan to explore the clinical use of FloVMos in oral imaging, which currently relies on a telescopic probe with a limited field of view due to space constraints. Our previous studies on videomosaicking [ 15 , 21 ] have shown its potential for increased imaging coverage. Integrating FM in this setting will provide real-time feedback to clinicians, enhancing imaging efficiency and diagnostic capabilities, ultimately improving patient outcomes.
